newsitem.title: DENMARK: Minister says Danish growth to accelerate.
newsitem.headline: Minister says Danish growth to accelerate.

text.p: Unveiling a new economic survey on Monday, Danish economy minister Marianne Jelved said that stagnation was over and a new upturn underway.
"The latest data confirms that the period of flat economic growth is now over," Jelved said in a statement accompanying her ministry's latest economic survey.

"Production, employment and investment are all showing solid growth and international surveys indicate that Denmark experienced the second biggest rise in the European Union in industrial production in the second quarter of 1996," she said.

The economy ministry survey surpassed earlier expectations of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to 2.0 percent in 1996 and 3.1 percent in 1997, compared to its last survey in August in which it forecast 1.8 percent and 3.0 percent respectively.

It kept its inflation forecasts more or less unchanged at 2.1 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year, with unemployment at 8.9 percent of the workforce in 1996, falling to 8.4 percent at end-1997.
In addition the ministry said it expected Denmark's current account surplus to be 10.3 billion danish crowns ($1.75 billion) in 1996, rising marginally to 10.8 billion crowns next year.

Jelved said that Denmark satisfied the convergence criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) despite the fact that it had already rejected the project and a referendum would have to be held on any future Danish participation.
Jelved warned though that there were dangerous trends in Denmark's economic upturn and promised moves to curb in particular public building and construction projects.
"This is a signal that we must take seriously. To avoid any overheating of the economy the government is taking steps to dampen public sector building programmes," she said.
She reiterated that the government's target of balancing the public sector budget in 1997 was still possible.
The survey saw the public sector deficit for this year at 14.9 billion crowns, falling to a manageable 3.5 billion crowns next year.

"A balanced 1997 public sector budget is within our grasp and this will be one of the government's main targets to be realised in the upcoming negotiations with opposition parties on the 1997 state budget," Jelved stressed.
Denmark's 1997 state budget is to be passed by Christmas following negotiations between the Social Democrat-led centre-left minority government and opposition parties due to start this month.
